latin: Jōsēphus. — Quid adeō tē sollicitat, pater? Maerōre<sup>1</sup> vīderīs ultrā<sup>2</sup> mōrem occupātūs.
Pater. — Enimvērō<sup>3</sup> tabellāriī hōra est, nōnne?
J. — Ita, profectō. Quid inde<sup>4</sup> nōn capiō.
P. — Āh, fīlī mī! nescīsne quattuor ipsōs esse diēs ex quō Antōnius perīcula<sup>5</sup>, Barcinōne<sup>6</sup>, subīre* dēbuit, necdum ad nōs litterārum quicquam<sup>7</sup>.
J. — Equidem nōn putāram<sup>8</sup>. Certō, pater, scrībere potuerat.
P. — Quīn immō<sup>9</sup>, sī bene omnia cessissent, et apud nōs esse. Pulsantur forēs<sup>10</sup> ā tabellāriō.
J. — Ad nōs tabellārius! Ē vestīgiō<sup>11</sup> currō. Ad vestibulum domūs properat.
P. dēsuper fīlium adloquitur. — Numquidnam bonī, Jōsēphe?
J. — Antōnius, Antōnius quī scrīpsit ipse. Dēmitte centēsimās trīgintā quās tabellāriō tribuam.
P. — Trāde mihi epistulam: involūcrum ego aperiam.
Vōce jūcundā: «Antōnius Patrī suō cārissimō salūtem dat. Mātūrius<sup>12</sup> scrībere optābam; quod quidem nōn licuit.
Cēterum<sup>13</sup> fausta<sup>14</sup> omnia. Lauream sum adsecūtus. Tramīne adveniam quod nōnae pūnctō Barcinōne discēdit. Valē mī pater<sup>15</sup>!
Datum Barcīnōne, diē Jūniī vīcēsimō sextō.»
Deō grātiās! Nunc dēmum animum recipiō.

J. — Ita, proféctō. Quid inde<sup>4</sup> nōn cápiō.

P. dḗsuper fī́lium adlóquitur. — Numquídnam bonī, Jōsḗphe?
J. — Antṓnius, Antṓnius quī scrīpsit ipse. Dēmítte centḗsimās trīgíntā quās tabellā́riō tríbuam.
P. — Trāde mihi epístulam: involū́crum ego apériam.
Vōce jūcúndā: «Antṓnius Patrī suō cāríssimō salū́tem dat. Mātū́rius<sup>12</sup> scrī́bere optā́bam; quod quidem nōn lícuit.

Datum Barcīnṓne, diē Jū́niī vīcḗsimō sextō.»
Deō grā́tiās! Nunc dēmum ánimum recípiō.
english: Joseph. — What is worrying you so much, papa? You seem [more preoccupied] (busy) by [worry] than [usual] (beyond habit).
The father. — [Isn't it] the postman's time?
J. — Yes, certainly. [I don't see the connection] (what from there I don't grasp).

F. — Ah, my son! Don't you know [that it is] four days [already] (themselves to be) since Antoine had to sit his exams in Barcelona, [and still no letter for us] (and not yet towards us of letter anything)?
J. — As for me, I hadn't thought of it. Certainly, papa, he could have (had been able to) written.
F. — And even, if all (things) [had gone well], [he would have been] with us. [The postman knocks at the door] (the doors are knocked by the postman).
J. — The postman [is coming] to us! I'll run [straight away] (from the spot). — He hurries to the entrance hall of the house.
F., calling his son from above. — Is it something good, Joseph?
J. — It's Antoine, Antoine who wrote himself. Send down 30 centimes that I'll give to the postman!
F. — Give me the letter: [it's] me [who] will open the envelope.
In a joyful voice: «Antoine [greets] (gives greeting) his very dear father. I wanted to write earlier, which however was not [possible] (permitted).

[Besides] [everything] (all things) [is going] very [well] (happy). I have [passed] (obtained the laurel). I will arrive by the train which leaves Barcelona at nine [o'clock] (on the dot). Look after yourself, my dear papa!
[Done] (given) in Barcelona, 26 June.»
[Thanks] be to God! Now at last I [take heart again] (my mind I take back).

footnotes: Maeror, -oris, m., grief, sorrow; the corresponding adjective is maestus, -a, -um, afflicted.
Enimvero, conj., in fact, indeed, for sure.
Inde, adv., from there; corresponds to the question unde?, whence?, from where?, whose answer can be: hinc, istinc, illinc, from here (from there) where I am, where you are, where he is.
Periculum, -i, n., danger, peril, or examination. This bugbear expression only frightens those who do not know ASSIMIL!
Barcino, -onis, Barcelona; ablative having the value of a locative.

Subire* = sub + ire, irregular verb, conjugated like ire. Quisquam, someone; quidquam or quicquam, something; this adjective pronoun has no feminine. Note that litterarum is a genitive. Likewise below (P. 8): (num) quidnam, what then?
Putaram, abridged form of putaveram (ind. p.q.p.).
Quin immo: quin, adv., why not? (quin loqueris?, why don't you speak?); immo, adv., on the contrary, rather (cf. L. 66, N. 5, quin etiam, same sense).
Fores, -ium, f. pl., the double leaves of the door.
Vestigium, -ii, n., the trace, and sometimes (here), the instant.
Maturius, sooner, is an adverb constructed with the help of the neuter form of the comparative of the adjective maturus, -a, -um, ripe, precocious.
Ceterum, adv., which corresponds to the adjective pronoun ceteri, -ae, -a, the others, those of whom one has not spoken. This last adjective is only used in the plural.
Mi: vocative of the possessive pronoun meus, -a, -um. Mi pater is more familiar than pater mi, which simply means my father.
comments: Decedere, to leave; derived from cedere which you saw in phrase 6. — Careo, -es, -ere, -ui, v.i. + abl., to be deprived of. — Sors, sortis, is feminine.

latin: Cūr Desidērius maerōre adeō vidētur occupātus?
Socrus ejus ē vītā dēcessit: quā rē maestus est.
Hic est maeror magnus.
Majōris tamen est maerōris orbum patre aut mātre fierī.
Mihi omnium dolōrum maximus est pecūniā carēre.
Vir es turpis et cupidus: nōn cēterōrum miseriam, sed tantum fortūnam tuam cūrās.
Villicus est dīves agrīs.
Famulus, cui nūlla sunt bona, tamen contentus sorte suā vidētur.
Hominēs cīvitātī ūtilēs honōrantur, fūrēs autem dignī verbere in carcerem cōnjiciuntur.
Ut fūrēs in nūndinīs, ita inter sē intellegunt.
latinAccented: Cūr Desidḗrius maerṓre ádeō vidḗtur occupā́tus?
Socrus ejus ē vītā dēcéssit: quā rē maestus est.
Hic est maeror magnus.
Majṓris tamen est maerṓris orbum patre aut mātre fíerī.
Mihi ómnium dolṓrum máximus est pecū́niā carḗre.
Vir es turpis et cúpidus: nōn cēterṓrum misériam, sed tantum fortū́nam tuam cūrās.
Víllicus est dīves agrīs.
Fámulus, cui nūlla sunt bona, tamen conténtus sorte suā vidḗtur.
Hóminēs cīvitā́tī ū́tilēs honōrántur, fūrēs autem dignī vérbere in cárcerem cōnjiciúntur.
Ut fūrēs in nū́ndinīs, ita inter sē intéllegunt.
english: Why does Didier seem so absorbed by grief?
His mother-in-law has died (gone out of life): that is why he is sad.
It is a great sorrow.
However it is a greater sorrow [to become] an orphan of [one's] father or mother.
For me, the greatest sorrow is to be short of money.
You are a horrible and grasping man: you are not concerned with the misery of others, but only with your fortune.
The farmer is rich in lands.
The servant, to whom no goods belong, nevertheless seems content with his lot.
Men useful to the city are honoured; but thieves worthy of the whip are thrown into prison.
They get on like thieves at a fair.
